cues.text: Welcome everyone, today we talk about running streaming pipelines at scale.
Let us start with what a topic really is.
A topic is an ordered log that producers append to.
Every topic is split into partitions.
Each partition is an append only sequence of records.
Records in a partition get a sequential offset.
Offsets are only meaningful inside one partition.
Ordering is guaranteed per partition, not per topic.
So the choice of record key matters a lot.
Records with the same key always land in the same partition.
Now let us look at producers.
A producer batches records before sending them.
Batching trades a little latency for much better throughput.
The linger setting controls how long a batch may wait.
Compression is applied to a whole batch.
Fast codecs usually win on busy clusters.
Acknowledgements decide how safe a write is.
With all replicas acknowledged, a write survives a broker crash.
Idempotent producers remove duplicates caused by retries.
Transactions extend that guarantee across several partitions.
Next come the brokers.
A broker stores partitions on local disk.
Each partition has one leader and several followers.
Followers copy records from the leader.
The in sync replica set tracks which followers are caught up.
If a leader fails, one of the in sync followers takes over.
Replication factor three is a common default.
Disk throughput usually limits a broker before the network does.
Page cache does most of the work for recent reads.
Keep the heap small and leave memory to the operating system.
Now we turn to consumers.
Consumers read records by asking the broker for an offset.
A consumer group shares the partitions of a topic.
Each partition is read by exactly one member of a group.
Adding consumers beyond the partition count does not help.
When membership changes, the group rebalances.
Rebalances pause consumption for a short time.
Static membership avoids many unnecessary rebalances.
Committed offsets record where a group stopped reading.
Committing after processing gives at least once delivery.
Committing before processing risks losing records.
Exactly once needs transactions or idempotent sinks.
Let us talk about retention.
Records are deleted by age or by total size.
Compacted topics keep only the latest value for each key.
Compaction suits changelogs and configuration data.
Tombstones are records with a null value.
They tell compaction to forget a key entirely.
Segment size controls how often old data can be removed.
Small segments mean many files and more overhead.
Large segments delay cleanup and recovery.
Retention is a business decision, not only a technical one.
Now the interesting part, stream processing.
A stream processor reads topics and writes new topics.
Stateless operations like filter and map are easy to scale.
Stateful operations need local storage.
Aggregations keep a running value for each key.
That state lives in a local store next to the task.
The store is backed up to a changelog topic.
After a crash, the task rebuilds its state from that topic.
Standby replicas make recovery much faster.
Joins combine two streams by key and by time.
A windowed join only matches records close in time.
Windows can be tumbling, hopping or session based.
Late records are a fact of life in distributed systems.
A grace period decides how long to wait for stragglers.
After that, late records are dropped or sent aside.
Event time is almost always better than processing time.
Timestamps come from the producer unless configured otherwise.
Watermarks are not used here, stream time just moves forward.
Stream time advances with the newest record seen.
Idle partitions can hold back progress.
Keep an eye on that when traffic is uneven.
Let us move on to schema management.
Records are bytes, so everyone must agree on the format.
A schema registry stores versions of each schema.
Producers register a schema and send only its identifier.
Consumers fetch the schema by that identifier.
Compatibility rules protect readers from breaking changes.
Adding an optional field is usually safe.
Removing a required field is not.
Plan schema changes like you plan database migrations.
Test them against real data before rolling them out.
Now let us talk about operations.
Monitoring starts with consumer lag.
Lag is the distance between the newest offset and the committed one.
A growing lag means consumers cannot keep up.
Under replicated partitions signal a struggling broker.
Watch request latency at the broker and the client.
Alert on trends, not on single spikes.
Capacity planning begins with the write rate.
Multiply it by the replication factor and the retention.
That gives you the disk you need.
Leave at least thirty percent free space.
Rolling restarts keep the cluster available during upgrades.
Move one broker at a time and wait for replicas to catch up.
Partition reassignment moves data between brokers.
Throttle it so it does not starve live traffic.
Cruise control tools can automate the balancing.
Security deserves its own session, but a few words here.
Use encryption in transit between clients and brokers.
Authenticate every client with certificates or tokens.
Authorize access per topic with access control lists.
Never share one credential between many applications.
Rotate credentials on a regular schedule.
Let us finish with testing.
Unit test your topologies with a test driver.
Integration tests should use a real broker in a container.
Replay production traffic against a staging cluster.
Chaos tests reveal assumptions about failures.
Kill a broker and watch what your clients do.
Slow the network and see whether timeouts are sensible.
Document the results so the next team can learn from them.
To summarise, partitions are the unit of scale.
Keys decide ordering, and ordering decides correctness.
State needs a changelog and a plan for recovery.
Measure lag, plan capacity and test failures early.
Thank you for listening, and enjoy the rest of the conference.
Questions are welcome at the end of the hallway.
Slides and the sample code will be published next week.
